title: Enoch and Zion
hook: Moses 7 contains one of the most stunning images in all of scripture: the God of heaven weeping. Not metaphorically. Not symbolically. Weeping—over His children who refuse to come to Him. Enoch, granted a panoramic vision spanning creation to the Second Coming, sees the Father's tears and asks the question that echoes through mortality: 'How is it thou canst weep, seeing thou art holy, and from all eternity to all eternity?' The answer reveals the divine heart behind every covenant, every commandment, every call to repentance. This chapter doesn't just tell us about Zion—it shows us why Zion matters to the heart of God. It's the most emotionally intimate portrait of Deity in the Pearl of Great Price, and it comes through a prophet-seer most Latter-day Saints know only by name.
overview:
Moses 7 divides into two movements: Enoch's prophetic vision (verses 1-69) and the narrative conclusion of the City of Enoch (verses 13-21, 69). The Lord shows Enoch the span of human history—from Adam's posterity through the Flood, the meridian ministry of Christ, the Apostasy, and finally the Restoration and Millennium. Enoch sees not only events but emotions: the heavens weeping, Satan laughing, the earth groaning under wickedness. The chapter's emotional center is verses 28-41, where Enoch witnesses God's grief over His rebellious children and learns that divine omnipotence does not diminish divine pathos. God can weep precisely because He is holy—because His love is perfect, His pain over lost children is infinite. This is theology as relationship, not abstraction.

The chapter's central revelation is the doctrine of Zion, presented not as utopian fantasy but as the natural fruit of a people who 'were of one heart and one mind, and dwelt in righteousness; and there was no poor among them' (v. 18). Zion isn't built by superhuman saints but by covenant people who internalize celestial law until it becomes their nature. The text emphasizes both unity ('one heart') and equity ('no poor')—spiritual solidarity and economic consecration as two sides of the same covenant life. Enoch's city isn't raptured to escape hardship but translated because it has become incompatible with a telestial world. The vocabulary of translation—'Zion was not, for God received it unto himself'—echoes Genesis 5:24 and Hebrews 11:5, but Moses 7 gives the doctrine its fullest scriptural development.

The Lord's discourse to Enoch in verses 29-40 introduces theological concepts barely hinted at elsewhere in scripture. God identifies Himself as 'Man of Holiness' and His Son as 'Man of Counsel' (v. 35, footnote clarifies this is the Son of Man). The title 'Man of Holiness' appears nowhere else in canonized scripture and suggests that true holiness is inseparable from relational existence—God is holy precisely in His capacity for perfect relationship. The phrase 'God of nature' (v. 30) appears here uniquely, linking divine grief to the created order itself. This is not Greek apatheia, divine impassibility. This is the Hebrew understanding of a covenant God who binds Himself emotionally to His covenant people, who risks grief by granting agency.

Enoch's vision culminates in the Restoration and Millennium. He sees the latter-day gathering, the return of Zion, and the reunion of the celestial and terrestrial Zion (v. 63-64). The image of Enoch's Zion descending and the New Jerusalem ascending to meet—'and the Lord in the midst, and his glory shall be upon them'—is the scriptural source for multiple Doctrine and Covenants revelations about building Zion in the last days. The chapter ends not with Enoch's translation but with his continued prophetic ministry, being 'caught up into heaven' for further instruction (v. 69). This suggests that even translated beings continue to progress, continue to receive revelation, continue to be tutored by God.

The Christology of Moses 7 is pervasive but often overlooked. The suffering Savior foreseen in verses 45-47—who will be 'lifted up on the cross' and experience the pains of all people—is the same Being whose tears Enoch witnesses. The God who weeps in verse 28 is Jehovah, the premortal Christ. His tears in the primeval council prefigure His blood in Gethsemane. Both express the depth of divine love and the cost of divine justice mercifully satisfied. Enoch learns that the Atonement isn't a legal transaction performed by an emotionally distant judge but the self-sacrifice of a God who weeps over every soul lost and rejoices over every soul redeemed.

key_verses.text_kjv: And the Lord called his people Zion, because they were of one heart and one mind, and dwelt in righteousness; and there was no poor among them.
key_verses.insight: This is the scriptural definition of Zion—not a location but a condition. The three-fold criteria (unity, righteousness, and equity) have become the template for every Latter-day Saint attempt to build Zion, from Kirtland to Jackson County to modern welfare programs. Notice that economic consecration ('no poor') isn't an add-on to spirituality but evidence of it.

key_verses.text_kjv: And it came to pass that the God of heaven looked upon the residue of the people, and he wept; and Enoch bore record of it, saying: How is it that the heavens weep, and shed forth their tears as the rain upon the mountains?
key_verses.insight: The only explicit description of God weeping in all of scripture. This verse has reshaped Latter-day Saint theology of God—refuting classical theism's impassible deity and revealing a God whose perfection includes, rather than excludes, the capacity for grief over His children's suffering and sin.

key_verses.text_kjv: And unto thy brethren have I said, and also given commandment, that they should love one another, and that they should choose me, their Father; but behold, they are without affection, and they hate their own blood;
key_verses.insight: God's lament reveals what breaks His heart: not just disobedience but lovelessness, the absence of affection among His children. The Hebrew concept here is chesed—loyal, covenantal love. Sin is redefined not primarily as rule-breaking but as the fracture of familial bonds, both vertical (with God) and horizontal (with each other).

key_verses.text_kjv: And behold, Enoch saw the day of the coming of the Son of Man, in the last days, to dwell on the earth in righteousness for the space of a thousand years;
key_verses.insight: Enoch's vision of the Millennium is explicitly connected to the Second Coming of Christ. The 'thousand years' mentioned here is one of the earliest scriptural attestations of a literal millennial reign, a doctrine that would be developed more fully in Revelation 20 and D&C 29.

key_verses.text_kjv: And righteousness will I send down out of heaven; and truth will I send forth out of the earth, to bear testimony of mine Only Begotten; his resurrection from the dead; yea, and also the resurrection of all men; and righteousness and truth will I cause to sweep the earth as with a flood, to gather out mine elect from the four quarters of the earth, unto a place which I shall prepare, an Holy City, that my people may gird up their loins, and be looking forth for the time of my coming; for there shall be my tabernacle, and it shall be called Zion, a New Jerusalem.
key_verses.insight: This verse is the scriptural fountainhead for multiple Latter-day Saint doctrines: the Book of Mormon coming 'out of the earth' as truth, the gathering of Israel in the last days, and the establishment of the New Jerusalem. Elder Bruce R. McConkie taught that 'righteousness' from heaven is the restoration of the gospel and priesthood, while 'truth' from the earth is the Book of Mormon itself.

highlights.snippet_text: The title 'Man of Holiness' for God the Father appears nowhere else in scripture. Joseph Smith's inspired translation reveals a relational God whose very title connects holiness to personhood—a direct refutation of the creeds' incomprehensible, unembodied deity. The Son is 'Man of Counsel,' suggesting the divine council prefigured in Abraham 3.
highlights.label: Restoration

highlights.snippet_text: The phrase 'one heart and one mind' reflects the Hebrew idiom lev echad—a unified will and purpose. This isn't enforced uniformity but the freely chosen harmony of people who have internalized the same divine law. The Nephite description of 4 Nephi uses nearly identical language, suggesting a scriptural template for covenant communities.
highlights.label: Hebrew

highlights.snippet_text: When God promises 'truth will I send forth out of the earth,' He's prophesying the coming forth of the Book of Mormon from the Hill Cumorah. Psalm 85:11 says 'truth shall spring out of the earth'—a passage Moroni may have known and saw fulfilled in his own ministry. The Book of Mormon title page echoes this very verse.
highlights.label: Cross-Ref

highlights.snippet_text: President Uchtdorf taught that these verses reveal 'the compassionate and loving nature of our Heavenly Father... God's anger is always and forever tempered by His infinite love and compassion.' The weeping God of Moses 7 transforms our understanding of divine justice—not cold calculation but heartbroken love seeking to save.
highlights.label: Prophetic

highlights.snippet_text: Enoch's continued ministry after translation parallels later Restoration teachings about translated beings. Joseph Smith taught that Enoch, Elijah, and others retain physical bodies to fulfill missions. D&C 133:54-55 confirms Enoch's return with his city at Christ's Second Coming—a nearly 5,000-year ministry spanning dispensations.
highlights.label: Historical

highlights.snippet_text: God's grief that His children are 'without affection' speaks directly to our social media age. When we reduce people to political categories, when we 'hate our own blood' over ideology, when families fracture over cultural divides—we reenact the very apostasy that made the heavens weep. Zion requires affection, not just orthodoxy.
highlights.label: Application

restoration_lens:
Moses 7 exists only because of Joseph Smith's inspired revision of Genesis. The entire Book of Moses—containing some of the most theologically rich material in Latter-day Saint canon—was given by revelation in 1830 as Joseph 'translated' the Bible. The Church had barely been organized when these visions of Enoch came. What the King James Bible dismisses in five verses (Genesis 5:18-24), the Prophet expanded into two full chapters. This wasn't speculation or commentary; Joseph said it came by 'the spirit of revelation,' restoring knowledge lost from the original text. The Book of Moses thus becomes Exhibit A for the necessity of continuing revelation and the incompleteness of the biblical record.

The doctrinal connections between Moses 7 and the Doctrine and Covenants are extensive and intentional. D&C 38:4 quotes God saying 'the same which have I taken unto mine own bosom'—a direct reference to Enoch's Zion. D&C 45:11-14 elaborates on the vision Enoch saw of the latter days, confirming that Enoch's prophecy of the New Jerusalem and the return of his city will literally be fulfilled. Section 84:99-100 speaks of Zion arising and putting on her beautiful garments, and the return of Enoch's people from their long translation. Section 133:56 even gives a purpose for Enoch's return: 'to prepare the way before the time of his coming.' These aren't loose parallels—these are explicit confirmations that Moses 7 is the foundation for Restoration Zion theology.

The temple connection is implicit but profound. The description of Enoch being 'caught up into heaven' and shown visions from beginning to end parallels the endowment's panoramic instruction. Hugh Nibley pointed out that Enoch's ascent, vision, and return to teach his people follows the ancient pattern of temple initiation found in Mesopotamian and Egyptian texts—the prophet-initiate ascends, sees the divine council, receives knowledge of past and future, and returns to establish a holy order among his people. The City of Enoch, dwelling 'in righteousness' with 'no poor among them,' represents the fullest expression of temple covenant living—what a community looks like when celestial law is collectively embraced. Every Latter-day Saint temple recommend interview asks if we're willing to consecrate our time, talents, and resources to building the kingdom—Enoch's people did exactly that, and the result was translation.
application:
Moses 7 confronts every Latter-day Saint with the gap between God's vision of Zion and our current reality. We speak often of building Zion, but do we grasp what the standard actually requires? 'One heart and one mind'—not casual association but deep unity of purpose. 'No poor among them'—not a welfare program we fund but a community where inequality is unthinkable because we genuinely see each other as family. The application isn't guilt but invitation: What would it look like for your ward, your family, your circle to move one degree closer to Zion's standard? The work begins in how we speak about the stranger, how we respond to the needy neighbor, how we choose unity over being right.

The weeping God of Moses 7 reframes every struggle with faith. When we wonder if God cares about our pain, this chapter answers: He cares to the point of tears. When we question whether our choices matter to an omnipotent Being, we learn that our agency to choose Him—or reject Him—matters enough to grieve the heart of Deity. For the parent with a wayward child, this is the most tender chapter in scripture: God knows exactly what you're feeling, because He's feeling it too, multiplied across billions of His children. The application isn't that God will force your child back—He doesn't force Enoch's rebellious brethren either—but that your heartbreak is shared by a God who will never stop reaching.

Finally, Moses 7 calls us to prophetic imagination. Enoch's vision spans from Creation to Millennium, helping him see his own moment in the context of God's entire plan. We live in the 'last days' Enoch foresaw, the era when 'righteousness and truth' would sweep the earth as a flood. Every missionary companionship, every temple session, every act of Christian service is part of the gathering Enoch saw. The application is to lift our eyes from the immediate crisis—political, personal, global—and see our covenant work in the sweep of dispensations. We're not just trying to survive mortality; we're participating in the final gathering before Enoch's Zion returns and meets the New Jerusalem. That vision doesn't diminish today's struggles; it sanctifies them as part of the grandest work in human history.
